Description: The application is built, verified, made available to the customer, and potentially deployable after every change. This does not require that the application is deployed after every delivery. Supporting documentation, such as release notes, are automatically generated to allow the Product Owner and customer to make an informed decision about making the updated application available to end-users. Since not every change may be deployed immediately, this documentation should make clear what changes occurred in each incremental version so all changes from an unknown previous version can be identified.
Prerequisites: Capability: Ops involved in cross-functional team
Capability: Decision criteria for release are fully automated
Questions: {id: Q300} Is the application delivered automatically to the customer or production environment from the pipeline? Note: not every change to the product may result in delivery or deployment; if necessary, there may be an approval process, but this approval process should require minimal intervention.
{id: Q301} Are changes since the previous deployment or delivery automatically generated and reported, for example in Release Notes?

Description: Team members carry out functional testing during development by running tests interactively. New changes are tested in an ad-hoc manner as a standard part of the edit-build-test cycle while the change is being implemented. There may be documented test cases for individual features or for the overall functionality of the application, but these test cases may be executed manually. Language-specific unit test systems (e.g., junit, gtest) may be used, but there is not necessarily a project-wide policy or consistency in their use. Before the application is delivered or deployed, there is a system test phase where the system is tested independent of the development activities and approved for release.
Questions: {id: Q8} Is there an independent system test phase that is carried out before delivery or deployment?

Description: The pipeline itself is monitored to support detection of failures, outages, and degradations to the pipeline and supporting services. The monitoring should support debugging issues and identifying unexpected side-effects of changes to the pipelines.
Questions: {id: Q184} Is the performance of the pipeline an input into planning for the environment?
{id: Q185} Are engineers notified of failures and service degradations to the pipeline and its supporting services?
{id: Q186} Are engineers easily able to plan for and track when pipeline services are upgraded?
{id: Q187} Can pipeline users view upcoming pipeline changes in a tracking tool?

Description: The pipeline and overall process is approved to support Continuous Delivery/Continuous Deployment. This may be in the form of a Continuous Authority to Operate (ATO) or equivalent. This requires ensuring that the processes for developing and deploying are sufficient, that they are followed, and that the automated tools generate sufficient evidence of the system’s security.
Prerequisites: Capability: Include security in cross-functional team
Questions: {id: Q294} Is a continuous ATO authority identified?
{id: Q295} Is the evidence generated by the pipeline sufficient to meet the continuous ATO requirements?
{id: Q296} Have the development, release, and deployment processes been approved to meet the continuous ATO requirements?
{id: Q297} Is there evidence to show that the development, release, and deployment processes have been followed?

Description: A security review is performed prior to application delivery. This may include activities such as a secure architecture review, a supply chain review of third-party components, and/or a vulnerability scan.
Questions: {id: Q12} Is there a documented security review plan?
{id: Q13} Is the security review performed prior to application delivery?
{id: Q14} Are deviations documented prior to application delivery?

Description: One purpose of Agile and DevSecOps software development is to maximize the opportunities for feedback. To accomplish this goal, small batches of value should be delivered to the customer regularly to elicit feedback.
Questions: {id: Q149} Does the product team deliver value to the customer frequently?
{id: Q150} Does the product team deliver small changes to the customer?

Description: The team monitors the system for operational issues such as application errors, service degradation, and resource utilization. The system should be monitored in all installed environments, but the method of monitoring may vary. For example, a development environment may have a monitoring dashboard which reports issues, while a production environment may have a dashboard as well as sending timely notifications to the team. The system and its environment must be engineered to support the monitoring requirements identified by the product team and product stakeholders.
Prerequisites: Capability: Ops involved in cross-functional team
Questions: {id: Q224} Is there a monitoring solution for operational issues?
{id: Q225} Does the team have access to monitoring data for all environments?

Description: The infrastructure is monitored for relevant security events. The exact events will vary based on environment and architecture, but may include events such as central processing unit (CPU) usage, network usage, network protocols used, changes in the infrastructure baseline, and more. These events should be analyzed to detect possible attacks by looking at metrics such as spikes in network traffic and failure to receive data from infrastructure components.
Questions: {id: Q260} Are behavior monitoring systems for the infrastructure and environment in place?
{id: Q261} Is sufficient data collected from infrastructure components for potential attacks to be detected?
{id: Q262} Are appropriate people notified if security issues are detected?

Capability: Security Scan of all External Packages before Mirroring
Description: As described in Capability: Artifact Management, external packages are mirrored internally and are imported or used from internal mirrors rather than directly from external sources. Before these packages are imported into the internal cache, they are scanned for security vulnerabilities; therefore, only scanned packages are included in CI builds of the product. Dependency Scanning tools are used; these recursively find all dependencies and check against a central database (e.g., National Institute of Standards and Technology [NIST] National Vulnerability Database [NVD]) for reported vulnerabilities. This includes not only packages used during building, but all dependencies including OS versions. If the packages are imported from a secure trusted source, then they do not need to be rescanned. The project, in cooperation with the AO, decides what are trusted sources. For example, a team may decide that official RedHat package repositories are trusted. Private developer builds may pull packages in directly from external sources; however, before those packages can be used in central CI builds, they will need to be imported into local mirrors and scanned appropriately.
Prerequisites: Capability: Security Policy is Defined for Third Party Components
Questions: {id: Q188} For every package in the internal cache, is there a record of the decision to accept the package? The record may show what actions were taken to approve the package, or it may simply state that the package (or all packages in the specific local mirror) are from a trusted source.
{id: Q189} Are package versions used by the application checked against a Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database of vulnerabilities, such as NVD, or equivalent?
{id: Q190} Is an automated supply chain vulnerability analysis tool used?

Description:
NIST defines five essential characteristics of cloud computing:

On-demand self-service

Broad network access

Resource pooling

Rapid elasticity

Measured service

Each developer has access to a cloud where they control the resources in use. There are pre-created cloud resources for central services such as ticket management systems or code quality scanners that maintain historical databases, but all other cloud resources are established and freed on demand.

This may not be applicable to all projects and may be tailored out if necessary.
Questions: {id: Q226} Does the team have access to create and modify nearly any cloud resource?
{id: Q227} Do cloud resources scale automatically as needed?
{id: Q228} Are cloud resources monitored by the team?

Capability: Responsibility for Release Decision is Documented
Description: The decision to release a new version of an application impacts engineers, the business, and end users. In some cases, this decision is carefully planned, while in other cases it may be on short-notice, such as for an urgent fix or security update. It is important that the authority and responsibility for making the release decision is clearly assigned and documented.
Questions: {id: Q63} Do the engineers know who is responsible for making release decisions?
{id: Q64} Do product stakeholders know who is responsible for making release decisions?
{id: Q65} Is the authority and responsibility for making a release decision clearly assigned and documented?

Description: The team needs to understand how much work they can accomplish within a development iteration. Initially this understanding may be inaccurate, but over time the understanding of how much work a team can accomplish in an iteration should become more predictable, based on experience and historical data. Once the capacity is understood, and work is consistently sized, the team can select work for each iteration based on their available capacity. The team should never commit to more work than their capacity allows.
Questions: {id: Q203} Does the team know how much work can be accomplished per iteration?
{id: Q204} Does the team commit to completing work that is within the understood capacity?
{id: Q205} Does the team adjust their capacity based on lessons learned in prior iterations?

Description: Stakeholders have input into the content, quality, and delivery of the application. These stakeholders may include: customer or customer representative; and the Authorizing Official (AO) or other security authority.
Questions: {id: Q18} Are the stakeholders identified?
{id: Q19} Is there a customer or customer representative among the stakeholders?
{id: Q20} Is there an AO or similar among the stakeholders?
{id: Q21} Have other possible stakeholders been considered?

Description: Teams that are provided the time, resources, and encouragement to experiment often produce more innovative solutions. These innovations may result in improvements to the product being developed or to the development process. Innovations that improve the team’s morale, reduces burnout, or improve the customer relationship are also valuable. To ensure that a team’s experimentation is productive, they should have access to information and context about the mission or business problems being faced. Additionally, they should be empowered to change stories, specifications, processes, and technologies in consultation with the product owner.
Prerequisites: Capability: Empowering teams to choose tools
Capability: Include security in cross-functional team
Questions: {id: Q246} Is the team empowered to pursue new ideas in pursuit of business goals that solve important problems?
{id: Q247} Does the team pursue innovation that improves team morale, reduces burnout, or improves customer relationships?

Description: DevSecOps leaders practice servant leadership where they demonstrate by example rather than tell the team how to behave. They focus on the team’s goals instead of their own, eliminating roadblocks so the team can be more effective. Servant leaders provide the goals for the team but trust the team to determine the best way to achieve those goals. Servant leaders should be responsive to the needs of their teams, and they help build a capable and adaptable team with the ability to change and evolve.
Questions: {id: Q206} Do leaders remove roadblocks that prevent the team from performing their best?
{id: Q207} Do leaders regularly listen to and respond to the needs of their team?
{id: Q314} Do leaders exhibit the ability to listen and understand?
{id: Q315} Do leaders exhibit the ability to accept and empathize with team challenges?
{id: Q316} Do leaders show foresight?
{id: Q317} Do leaders show awareness and perception?
{id: Q318} Does the team feel empowered to make decisions?

Capability: Definition of Done: Builds and Passes Tests
Description: A change is completed when the build completes without error or warnings and all defined tests and scans succeed. The build tools are configured to generate appropriate warnings and to fail if those warnings are generated. The team has reviewed warnings that can be generated by the build tools and agreed on appropriate settings.
Questions: {id: Q82} Do engineers understand that they should always complete a successful build of the codebase and pass all defined tests and scans before sharing the change with other engineers? Note: this is not a question about whether the engineers complete a successful build; this is about whether they know they should.
{id: Q83} Are tests written for every change?

Description: The system should be designed to take advantage of DevOps capabilities and principles during incident response. Any deployment or response automation should be designed to ensure forensic artifacts are maintained according to organizational policies. In addition, they should ensure that any automated remediation does not compromise the incident response process.
Prerequisites: Capability: Security involved in regular product reviews
Questions: {id: Q320} Has incident response been considered as part of defining the system requirements?
{id: Q321} Are forensic artifacts preserved when automated mitigations and/or remediations are triggered?
{id: Q322} Do incident responders have access to the DevOps tools necessary to contain, eradicate, and recover from an incident?

Capability: Decision Criteria for Release are Documented
Description: Any metrics or questions that are needed to make a release decision are defined and documented. This may include reports, visualizations, or data that need to be reviewed prior to a release.
Questions: {id: Q127} Are the release decision criteria documented?
{id: Q128} Does the person with release authority know how to retrieve data supporting the release decision criteria?
{id: Q129} Have product stakeholders’ recommendations been incorporated into the release decision criteria?
{id: Q130} Are engineers aware of the data required to support the release decision criteria?

Description: Failure analysis is the systematic process of determining the core issue that led to a problem being analyzed, for example, root cause analysis. While many issues may be uncovered during this process, the goal is to determine the initial trigger. Everyone involved in the process leading up to the problem is involved in the failure analysis.
Prerequisites: Capability: Testing/Quality Assurance (QA) Involved in Cross-Functional Team
Capability: Ops involved in cross-functional team
Capability: Include security in cross-functional team
Questions: {id: Q217} Does the product team conduct failure analysis of problems discovered in production?
{id: Q218} Are the members of the product team that were involved in the process leading up to the problem included in the failure analysis?
{id: Q219} Does the product team  determine how to prevent or mitigate the root causes of the failure?
{id: Q220} Does the product team track this change to ensure it is implemented?

Description: There is an automated build that runs at least once a day and that builds the latest version of code on any release branch. If there are no changes, the build may still run to check that any external dependency changes do not affect the build. Engineers have the responsibility for not breaking the build on release branches. If the pipeline does break e.g., if the build fails, if any of the required tests fail, or if automated scans fail to pass project criteria, then it becomes a top priority for the team to fix the failure or to back out the change if a fix is not possible in a reasonable amount of time. An important Agile principle is respect for the engineers on the team. If the pipeline fails, this is not a reason to blame the engineer responsible. Instead, the team works together as responsible and professional engineers to find the issue and resolve it, and to take steps to prevent the same problem from happening again.
Questions: {id: Q84} Is there an automated build that runs every time a change is merged into the release branch?
{id: Q85} Is an automated notification sent to engineers when the pipeline build fails?
{id: Q86} When the CI build fails, is it a top priority for the team to fix the build?

Description: The application can be deployed automatically using IaC to a dynamically created target environment. The pipeline creates test environments and deploys to those test environments. The test deployments are used for functionality and security scans, and for manual testing such as exploratory testing, usability testing, and acceptance testing. Developers can deploy private versions of the application to a private test environment.
Questions: {id: Q234} Does the pipeline deploy to a newly created test environment?
{id: Q235} Is the test environment used by the pipeline to run automated tests?
{id: Q236} Is there a separate test environment that can be used for interactive testing, such as exploratory or usability testing?

Description: The supported environment, including development environments and pipelines, has a baseline of approved tooling that covers all common functions. The set of approved tooling is regularly reviewed by the team. The supported environment has the flexibility and processes in place to support requests from teams to adopt and support additional tools that were not previously in the approved set.
Questions: {id: Q231} Is there a common, supported set of tools that covers all common functions, such as build orchestration, compilers, and scanners?
{id: Q232} Is the common set of tools reviewed regularly to determine if it meets the current requirements of the project and to determine if there are other tools that could be added?
{id: Q233} Is there a process in place to allow the team to request adoption of other tools to enhance the engineering environment?

Description: At regular intervals, the team takes time to reflect on their accomplishments and failures to determine how to become more effective. These proposed changes are added to the work backlog, tracked, and implemented in future intervals. The team should reflect upon how effective the changes were and modify their work accordingly.
Questions: {id: Q208} Does the team regularly reflect on their successes and failures and determine how they can improve?
{id: Q209} Do the improvement ideas get added to the backlog?
{id: Q210} Does the team work on the improvement ideas?
{id: Q211} Does the team review the results of the improvement changes and make additional changes as needed?

Description: Applications can be deployed automatically to a test environment. The test environment may contain pre-created artifacts, such as a VM, for deployment. This is typically used in a pipeline where there is guaranteed to be one build/test pipeline running at a time. Internet Protocol (IP) addresses and other configuration details can be hard-coded.
Questions: {id: Q196} Does the pipeline always deploy the application to a test environment that is only used for system tests?
{id: Q197} Is the usage of the dedicated test environment well-defined and understood?

Description: The pipeline’s output and results are monitored to support detection of failures, outages, and degradations (e.g., lower testing coverage). The monitoring should be comprehensive enough to allow debugging any issues.
Prerequisites: Capability: Continuous functional testing and scanning
Questions: {id: Q180} Are there limits or other acceptance criteria for test coverage, scanning results, and other quantifiable pipeline results?
{id: Q181} Is a failure to adhere to the limits or acceptance criteria reported to the team and to the scrum master?
{id: Q182} When limits or acceptance criteria fail, is action taken to resolve the issues?
{id: Q183} Are log files and other build artifacts kept for the most recent build on all release branches?

Description: Secure coding standards help ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the system being developed. By defining and following such standards, common vulnerabilities can be identified and avoided before they arise in production. It is easier and less costly to fix such vulnerabilities when they are found in development than in later stages of release.
Prerequisites: Capability: Version control for application source code
Questions: {id: Q104} Have secure coding standards been adopted?
{id: Q105} Do team members apply the secure coding standards during development?
{id: Q106} Do team members apply the secure coding standards during peer-review of code?

Description: The application can be deployed automatically and with minimal impact to users. This requires a documented and automated strategy for deployments. Examples include Blue/Green deployment with user ramping and Canary deployment with percentage-based replacement. Deployments do not change existing systems but should replace existing systems in accordance with the principles of immutable configuration.
Questions: {id: Q284} Can updates to the application be deployed to a production environment without requiring any downtime for the application?
{id: Q285} Does the strategy for deploying updates to the application follow the concept of immutable configuration?
{id: Q286} Is the application deployment strategy documented and automated?

Description: Each work item has associated acceptance criteria. The acceptance criteria list the requirements each work item must meet in support of the objectives of the product. This may include both functional and non-functional criteria which deliver value to the customer. Acceptance Criteria in the definition of done help the team know when they are finished developing a work item. Meeting the acceptance criteria is only one part of meeting the definition of done for a work item.
Questions: {id: Q100} Does each work item have acceptance criteria defined before work starts?
{id: Q101} Are the acceptance criteria clear about the requirements for the product?
{id: Q102} Are the acceptance criteria met before the work item is accepted as done?
{id: Q103} Do the acceptance criteria help ensure the work being done furthers the product’s objectives?

Description: There is an automated method for system recovery after a failure. This requires identifying that a failure has occurred, as well as recovering from it. The extent of the recovery may depend on the failure. For example, recovery after a database upgrade may be a rollback to the previous known-good state. Automated recovery from failure should not preclude logging, and, if appropriate, alerting on the initial failure.
Questions: {id: Q278} Does the monitoring system identify failures which can be recovered from via automation?
{id: Q279} Is there automation for recovering from the most common types of failures?
{id: Q280} Is there automation for recovering from the most disruptive types of failures?
{id: Q281} Does the automated recovery process preserve data on the failure for further analysis, through logs or other methods?
{id: Q282} Does the automated recovery process generate appropriate logs or alerts on both the failure and recovery steps?
{id: Q283} Does a failure of the automated recovery process leave the system in a state which is no worse than after the initial failure?

Description:
The product team should follow these core principles: 

Adequate test data is available to run full automated tests. 

Test data for automated test suites can be acquired on demand. 

Test data is designed so it rarely restricts what automated tests teams can run, and any limitations are intentional and well understood. 

Tests do not depend on data or uncontrolled states external to the test. For example if a test requires e.g., the existence of a database, then either the dependency is satisfied with a stub, or the test creates and populates the database as part of the test. 

There may be (in fact there should be) system tests that run against a deployed version of the application. All information needed to set up such a deployment, including configuration details and data, are managed.
Questions: {id: Q164} Is there adequate test data to run full automated tests?
{id: Q165} Can test data for automated test suites be acquired on demand by the engineers for a private test run and for automated pipelines?
{id: Q166} Does the available test data limit or constrain the automated tests that teams can run?
{id: Q167} If there are staging or test deployment environments, is the creation of these environments fully automated including data population?

Description: The security monitoring systems for the application, infrastructure, and environment are unified to provide a single, consistent source of both data and alerting for the production system.
Questions: {id: Q269} Is there a unified way to view the security data for the complete system (including both the application and infrastructure)?
{id: Q270} Is the monitoring system configured so that data from the application supports alerts for the infrastructure and vice versa?
{id: Q271} Does the monitoring system avoid duplicate alerts for the same issue while still retaining the ability to alert on a single event?

Description: The application is monitored for relevant security events. The events will vary based on the application and architecture used, but may include events such as application failures, login successes/failures, access to administrative functionality, data exports, and more. These events should be analyzed to detect possible attacks by looking at metrics such as login failure rates and size of data exports.
Questions: {id: Q257} Are security monitoring systems for the application in place?
{id: Q258} Does the application generate sufficient data for potential attacks to be detected?
{id: Q259} Are appropriate people notified if security issues are detected?

Description: Developers have access to a shared cloud where they compete for and share resources. Developers may set up semi-permanent shared systems, such as a test deployment environment. The pipelines use pre-created cloud resources. This may not be applicable to all projects and may be tailored out if necessary.
Questions: {id: Q201} Do engineers have access to create/modify cloud resources?
{id: Q202} Does the pipeline run on cloud resources?

Capability: Decision Criteria for Release are Fully Automated
Description: Automating the release criteria and their supporting evidence helps improve not only the speed at which a system can be released, but also the speed of feedback cycles to the product team if there are any deficiencies. Additionally, automation ensures that the release criteria are applied consistently for every potential release.
Prerequisites: Capability: Release decisions are evidence-based and supported by measurable results
Questions: {id: Q298} Is the supporting evidence for each release criterion generated by the CI/CD pipeline?
{id: Q299} Are the results for each release criterion determined automatically from the supporting evidence?

Description: Maintainability standards are set and followed. These standards may include limits on complexity, standardized formatting, and other “code smells” that make it difficult to maintain code over time. Tools are used to the extent possible to identify improvement opportunities. For some classes of issues, tools may also automatically remediate issues (e.g., a linter that automatically reformats files to meet the standard).
Questions: {id: Q137} Has the team documented and agreed on coding standards?
{id: Q138} Do the coding standards include how source code will be formatted?
{id: Q139} Do the coding standards include complexity metrics?
{id: Q140} Do the coding standards include rules to encourage readability of code?
{id: Q141} Are automated tools being used to identify code that does not meet the standards?
{id: Q142} Are code documentation standards set?
{id: Q143} Do all engineers know where to find the coding and documentation standards?
{id: Q144} Is code that does not meet standards promptly improved?

Description: The system has clean, well-defined interfaces between loosely coupled components. Principles such as Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) are followed. This encourages improvements in testability resulting in better quality. It also allows multiple team members to develop simultaneously with minimal impact to each other, to stable components, and to external partners. The architecture should be well documented and kept up to date to aid in future development and maintenance of the system.
Questions: {id: Q131} Is architecture considered during planning?
{id: Q132} Are separate components clearly identified?
{id: Q133} Is the architecture documented?
{id: Q134} Is the documented architecture kept up to date?
{id: Q135} Does the architecture allow several engineers to work on the system simultaneously with minimal impact to each other?
{id: Q136} Does the architecture provide external partners a stable interface/API?

Description: The production environment is monitored in real time for indications of security breaches or risks. This can include monitoring for unexpected configuration changes, or unusual behavior or requests. The environment is not only monitored for actual security breaches, but also proactively for issues that might indicate a pending problem. When security issues are identified by the monitoring system, notifications are sent to the appropriate people.
Questions: {id: Q263} Are real-time security monitoring systems for the production environment, including the application, in place?
{id: Q264} Do the security monitoring systems generate real-time alerts when issues, or potential issues are detected?
{id: Q265} Are appropriate people notified if security issues are detected?

Description: Leadership is critical to being successful with DevSecOps. At the beginning of DevSecOps adoption, leadership provides a strong vision and the psychological safety to allow team members to fail at tasks without negative consequences. As teams mature in their DevSecOps journey, leadership continues to provide support and recognition to teams. Even highly performing teams benefit from leadership practices which further encourage and intellectually challenge them to strive for relentless, continuous improvement. The methods by which leaders support their teams may vary, however clear communication at all times is critical. Some common methods include coaching, training, recognition, and seeking out intellectual challenges.
Questions: {id: Q287} Do team members feel motivated?
{id: Q288} Do team members feel confident that the team is structured for success?
{id: Q289} Do team members feel that they are valued as individuals in the team?
{id: Q290} Are team members encouraged to learn and apply new skills?
{id: Q291} Do team members have specified personal goals, and are they rewarded for meeting or exceeding those goals?
{id: Q292} Do leaders remove roadblocks that prevent the team from performing their best?
{id: Q293} Do team members feel confident raising problems and admitting failures?
{id: Q319} Do leaders show foresight?

Description: In continuous deployment, the application is not only regularly delivered to production by automation, but deployed and made available to end users without manual intervention. As is clear from the many dependencies for this capability, this requires exceptionally strong application development practices, automation, and understanding of the business processes the application supports.
Questions: {id: Q302} Can the application be deployed directly to production after passing the CI/CD pipeline, without manual intervention?
{id: Q303} Can the application be made available to production users after passing the CI/CD pipeline, without manual intervention?

Description: Backlog Management, sometimes called backlog refining or grooming, ensures the most valuable product is released to customers. It involves reviewing, reevaluating, and reprioritizing pending work items with input from the customer. Backlog management can be done for the sprint, release, or, project. Requests for new features and enhancements to existing functionality can be added to a backlog and ranked based on mission value. Determining which type of backlog to use helps the team deliver against the product roadmap in an incremental and iterative way. Examples of backlogs include a product backlog that lists features that are requested but may not be prioritized, release backlog that includes features for an identified release, and sprint backlog that includes stories identified for a sprint.
Questions: {id: Q78} Does the team include features, bug fixes, and infrastructure changes in the project backlog?
{id: Q79} Are the backlog items detailed at a level that the team can size the work?
{id: Q80} Is there a plan to reprioritize the backlog at regular intervals to accomodate changes?
{id: Q81} Are the customer or stakeholders involved when prioritizing the backlog?

Description: The codebase is divided into separate modules, with well-defined interfaces between the modules. Each module has a well-understood purpose and behavior. Each module can be tested independently, by stubbing out required modules. Different modules do not need to be managed in different source code repositories. One source code repository can manage multiple, if not all, modules in a project; however, in this case the source code, tests, and build files for each module may be organized in separate directories.
Questions: {id: Q51} Is there a defined directory structure for software modules?
{id: Q52} Does the defined directory structure include unit and functional tests?
{id: Q53} Does the defined directory structure document/define the provided interfaces for a module, (e.g., header files for libraries, OpenAPI/Swagger or similar specifications for services)?
{id: Q54} Is there a hierarchical build system where modules are built separately (possibly in a build dependency order), then combined into the application?

Description: Feedback from the customer and end users is solicited to drive future development.
Questions: {id: Q304} Is feedback solicited from the customer about the deployed application?

Description: Notifications are sent to the team when warning signs are detected that correlate with application failures. Actual failures also alert the team but are not sufficient to meet this capability. Examples of warning alerts may include high resource use which may lead to application errors or a sudden drop in serviced requests which may indicate a networking error.
Questions: {id: Q239} Is the team notified of application failures?
{id: Q240} Does the team identify application warning thresholds that indicate incipient application failure?
{id: Q241} Is the team notified when application warning thresholds are crossed?
{id: Q242} Do application warning notifications generally provide the team enough time to intervene before application failure?

Capability: Definition of Done: Customer Acceptance in Production
Description: A change is completed when it has been delivered to and accepted by the customer in a deployed environment. If the change is not a customer-impacting issue, then the change is completed when the original initiator or the role impacted by the change accepts the change. For example, a new scanning tool may be added to the CI pipeline; the work item used to track adding the tool will be closed when it is demonstrated that the tool is properly integrated into the pipeline and any metrics from the tool are accessible and can be used by the team.
Prerequisites: Capability: Definition of done: Passes pipeline
Questions: {id: Q212} Do work items remain in a non-completed state until the customer or other initiator of the work item accepts the work item resolution?

Description: The value stream is the series of steps taken to get a customer’s idea into their hands. For software development this includes all the steps from requirements elicitation through deployment. Each software product may have a different value stream, based on the unique needs of that product. For example, a product that is in maintenance mode may rely less upon requirements or design steps, since the majority of work being done is bug fixes. The team understands how work moves through the various steps, beginning and ending with the customer. This flow is modeled and tracked through the  team’s work board.
Questions: {id: Q66} Does the product team understand all the steps needed to deliver work to the customer?
{id: Q67} Does the team board reflect all these steps?

Description: At regular intervals, the team takes time to reflect on their accomplishments and failures and to determine how to become more effective. For changes that have been implemented, the team should reflect upon how effective the changes were and modify their work accordingly.
Questions: {id: Q15} Does the team regularly reflect on their successes and failures and determine how they can improve?
{id: Q16} Does the team implement the improvement ideas?
{id: Q17} Does the team review the results of the improvement changes and make additional changes as needed?

Description: The CI pipeline should be secured, and mitigation plans developed for any risks that cannot be prevented. For example, the CI pipeline should only be accessible to authorized users. In addition, a mitigation plan should be developed for minimizing the damage malicious code run by an authorized user can cause.
Questions: {id: Q87} Has the security of the CI pipeline been evaluated?

Description:

Holding regular lunch-and-learn sessions where one team member shares knowledge about a current project or a particular tool or technology. 

Encouraging team members to attend or present at conferences. 

Providing financial assistance for formal external training and certifications. 

Budgeting for a certain number of hours each week to be spent on personal improvement, exploration, and learning. 

Creating a site or other repository for lessons learned. 

The learning culture is supported by the organization at all levels and leadership understands that resources assigned and used for learning are an important part of general team improvement.

Description:
There is a branching and merging strategy that is used by all software engineers. The strategy defines a way to separate development work, which can be unstable, from stable branches that are updated in a controlled way and that should always have a defined level of quality. It also defines how changes flow between the branches, including any required quality controls such as code reviews, testing, and security scans as changes are merged from less stable (development) branches to more stable (release) branches. 

The details of the branching and merging strategy will depend heavily on many project-dependent factors, including:

- Size of the codebase: if the complete codebase fits into one repository, then the branching strategy can be relatively simple. However, if the codebase spans multiple repositories with dependencies between the repositories, then it is important to understand how the branching in one repository corresponds to the branching in a different repository. In the latter case if there is a well-defined application programming interface (API) between the components then it may be necessary to maintain support for older API versions using maintenance branches.

- Size of the product team: if the team is small and each change is typically worked on by one engineer, then that engineer can work in a local workspace which may or may not correspond to a branch and push when the change is complete; if the team is large and many engineers typically work together on a change then they will need a dedicated development branch where they can share a common work environment. 

- Version control tool: A Distributed Version Control System (DVCS) such as git has local workspaces or repo clones that are isolated from the central managed repository and that can effectively act as branches. A centralized version control system, such as ClearCase, requires a new, centrally managed branch to ensure any isolation of changes. 

- Application lifecycle: An application such as a web site that is deployed (continuously or discretely) to one production environment will typically have one release branch that is regularly deployed; An application with multiple external customers will typically have to maintain multiple older releases each on its own maintenance branch. In the case that multiple maintenance branches exist, the strategy must address ensuring that fixes are applied to all relevant branches. Lifetime of the application: if the product team is working on a series of short-lived applications, each created from scratch using a fresh codebase, then there can be one simple branching strategy that is reused repeatedly; if the application is long-lived then the branching strategy needs to allow for additional complexity.
Prerequisites: Capability: Version control for application source code

Description: The branching and merging strategy, in combination with the pipeline, ensures that release branches are normally releasable, i.e., they have sufficient quality to be deployed to the production environment. This is an essential prerequisite for Continuous Delivery (CD). The pipeline must also ensure that successful and releasable builds are identified in the version control system. If a change does cause the pipeline to fail, then these criteria are revisited to see if the same problem could be prevented in the future. The CI pipeline has sufficient automated tests to ensure that a build has sufficient quality to be released. This does not mean that any build could be released to the customer, just that if the pipeline succeeds then the quality of the codebase is known. The branching strategy includes bugfix management, guaranteeing that any individual bugfix is implemented on all affected branches.
Prerequisites: Capability: Definition of Done: Acceptance Criteria

Description: All automated test scripts and other files, including test data, are managed in version control. Test time dependencies on external systems are minimized or ideally eradicated. Some testing and reporting frameworks such as Selenium or SonarQube require pre-configured external servers, but in these cases the details of the configuration are managed in the pipeline orchestrator rather than in the source codebase. This affords the opportunity for the supporting environment to be reconfigured without impact on the codebase. Scanning tools, used to find security vulnerabilities, code issues, embedded secrets, and policy violations are run by the pipeline. Any supporting files that are specific to the application are managed in version control. The defined build environment supports running automated tests and code scanning tools.
Prerequisites: Capability: Testing/Quality Assurance (QA) Involved in Cross-Functional Team

Description: All work is tracked in a tool, and the team has a way to visually represent the state of this work. The tool used to track work should be able to accommodate this need.

Capability: Security Policy is Defined for Third Party Components
Description: The inclusion of third-party components, such as libraries or APIs, introduces risk to a system. The risk may be in running unverified code, malicious updates, or simple unavailability of a critical component. A policy defining how to evaluate third-party components before including them in the system helps to manage these risks. This policy should be simple and clear enough for the development team to evaluate multiple components on a regular basis as new business needs arise.

Description: Security scanning and other tests, standardized and custom, are included in the regular pipeline tests. This improves visibility and shortens the feedback cycle for many security concerns. When integrating into the pipeline, the pass/fail thresholds must be carefully considered to provide the right balance between security assurance and not overloading the team with false positives.

Description: The Product Roadmap sets forth the major efforts needed to achieve the overall business objectives and timeline for implementing features that align with the vision and strategy. It should not include strategic ideas, feature requests, product backlog items, and defects. It should include the vision for the product, the future direction for evolution of the product, and short- and long-term priorities. Additionally, the product roadmap should track the current progress towards these goals. It should be considered as an evolving artifact and a collaboration aid to assist in communicating the focus and priorities throughout the lifecycle of the product. Contributions to the product roadmap should include customer, stakeholder, and team members’ feedback.

Capability: Release Decisions are Evidence-Based and Supported by Measurable Results
Description: Release decisions should be based on both the value of releasing the system and on data demonstrating confidence in the system’s performance once released. Description: Environments used to build, test, and deploy the application are defined using Infrastructure as Code (IaC). The code used to define the environments is managed alongside the application source code in version control and is used during development, testing, and deployment of the application. A cloud-based application will use CloudFormation, Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates, Ansible, or similar tools to define the environments. An application targeted to run on a server may use VM or container images as the environments, and these images are built using version-controlled files. An embedded application will have a defined build environment but may not have defined test or deployment environments.

The releases should be frequent (e.g., timeboxed to atleast monthly) and iterative, to increase the opportunities for feedback. Description: The infrastructure that supports the application is monitored for issues that may affect performance or availability of the application. This includes (but is not limited to) the physical health of the hardware, system parameters such as utilization of disk, processors and memory, and network utilization. Events and logs for all infrastructure components are also monitored, and thresholds are established for operational parameters. There is a dashboard or other mechanism that displays the current operational status of the infrastructure, including highlighting issues or potential issues. Historical data is also available so that, for example, it is possible to distinguish between a disk that has slowly been filling up for the last six months versus a disk that went from 10 percent full to 90 percent full in the last five minutes. There is a notification system so that relevant people are notified automatically when particular events occur, or thresholds are passed. When possible, the team should correlate events and measures to gain insight into possible root causes for issues.

Description: Decisions, including change approvals, are made at the most specific level that still addresses all key stakeholders. However, they now engage earlier in defining changes to be made and are no longer used to approve changes before release.

Description: The objectives, or goals, for a product are understood and documented. These objectives reflect the value the organization gets out of the product, not necessarily the requirements needed to complete the product. For example, a website may be built to communicate or to allow users to complete transactions quickly. These objectives define why a product is being built or improved and can be used by the product owner and the team to ensure all work is progressing towards these objectives. These objectives may change over time in response to customer demand and external changes. When objectives change, they should be communicated to the entire team and documented

Description: Security as a final pre-release gate has been shown to be less effective than performing frequent security reviews during product development. This may include review of both architecture and code.

Description: Database schema changes are handled using version-controlled files, and repeatable and testable processes (for example, as a series of migration scripts that must be applied in order). There may also be version-controlled and repeatable methods to reverse a schema change.

Description: Velocity is a measure of the speed that it takes the team to complete their committed work. At the start of an iteration the team commits to complete a certain number of items of work, based on their capacity. The velocity is calculated by the size of each work item (e.g., completing an item of size 1 does not the affect the velocity as much as completing an item of size 5). The velocity line can be extrapolated based on what work has been completed in an iteration to inform the team as to whether they over committed or not.
Questions: {id: Q145} Does the team track the work items completed in each iteration?
{id: Q325} Are delivered work items compared to planned work items to ensure only approved changes are delivered?

{id: Q147} Does the team use the tracking to determine if they will complete their committed work for the iteration?
{id: Q148} Does the team use the tracking to inform their understanding of capacity?

Description: The production environment is monitored in real time for performance issues. This can include monitoring for resource shortages, slowness in transaction processing, slowness in database transactions, or any other issue that might indicate bottlenecks or other performance-affecting problems. The environment is not only monitored for actual issues, but also proactively for issues that might indicate a pending problem. In addition, business metrics collected by the monitoring system, for example, rates of particular function usage, should be shared with the Product Owner and used for determining future product improvements. When issues are identified by the monitoring system, notifications are sent to the appropriate people.
Questions: {id: Q266} Are real-time monitoring systems for the production application in place?
{id: Q267} Do the monitoring systems generate real-time alerts when issues, or potential issues are detected?

Description: Communications between the customer and the team clarifies the customer’s wants, needs, and expectations. Communications can include release notes, user stories, scheduled meetings, impromptu phone calls, email, posts on shared team channels, or any other form of communication between the team and the customer.

Description: The customer is represented during development to provide feedback on proposed implementations and priorities. At a minimum, the customer has an opportunity to give feedback once per development iteration or major feature. Often this takes the form of a feature demonstration from the product team. This feedback should focus on validating that the work being done will meet the mission needs of the customer in an efficient way. The feedback may be used to reprioritize the backlog or even add or remove planned features. A customer representative or product owner who is regularly communicating with the customer should also be involved in the planning and prioritization of work to ensure the planned work is likely to meet customer needs.
Questions: {id: Q198} Does the product team communicate with the customer during each development iteration or major feature (e.g., email, meetings, shared team channels)?

Capability: Scheduled Manual Deployment Reviews Including Security
Description: Whether or not security acts as a gate to deployment of a system, the security function can provide a valuable risk-based analysis of the impact of a release. This analysis should be included as part of manual deployment reviews prior to each release.
Questions: {id: Q44} Does security review the proposed release prior to its deployment?

Description:
For all release branches, a CI build is started whenever a change is promoted to the branch. The build may wait for a short grace period in case more changes are delivered to avoid multiple overlapping builds. Artifacts generated by the CI build are saved to an artifact management system as described in Capability: Artifact Management- Subsequent build stages use either files in the build tree or these saved artifacts, depending on the nature of the stage. For example, a deployment to a system test environment would use the packages from the artifact manager, while a code scanner would use source files in the build tree. The CI build includes several stages after building the application. Note: the build system should always run unit tests as an integral part of the build. After the build is completed one or more of the following activities should occur 

Security scans of the application and libraries 

Antivirus scans of the application and libraries Third-party code scans of the application and libraries 

Deploying the application to a test environment and system-level testing with automated tools, such as Selenium 

Packaging the application, libraries, and related documentation for delivery to the CDS.
Prerequisites: Capability: Continuous functional testing and scanning
Capability: Security scan of all external packages before mirroring
Questions: {id: Q191} Does every change delivered to a release branch trigger a CI build?
{id: Q192} Does the CI build run all applicable scanning tools?
{id: Q193} Does the CI build deliver deployable and labeled artifacts to the artifact management system?
{id: Q194} Does the CI build run system-level tests?

Description: A work item is done when it fully passes all stages in the pipeline. Once the CI pipeline is implemented and running, all promoted changes automatically start the CI pipeline. The pipeline is expected to always succeed; if it fails, then the focus of the team becomes fixing the build. If a change breaks the build in a way that cannot easily be fixed, the change will be pulled out of the branch.
Questions: {id: Q195} Does a change have to successfully run through the pipeline before it is considered complete?

Description: As part of the team’s Definition of Done, changes are considered complete and deliverable when the build completes without error. Only changes that build without error are pushed to the central shared repositories.
Questions: {id: Q27} Do engineers understand that they should always complete a successful build of the codebase before sharing the change with other engineers?  Note that this is not a question about whether they actually do complete a successful build, this is about whether they know they should.

Description: The team should hold itself accountable for the outcomes of their work. This includes delivering value to the business or mission their work supports, taking ownership of the quality of the product they support, and meeting their internal commitments (e.g., sprint commitments).

Description: The flow of value includes every step needed to get an idea from the head of the customer into the hands of the customer. The team should regularly identify ways to improve the flow of value by identifying bottlenecks, reducing handoffs, and identifying and reducing constraints. These improvements should be added to the team’s backlog to be worked, tracked like all other work, and implemented in future intervals
Prerequisites: Capability: Include security in cross-functional team
Questions: {id: Q221} Does the team identify bottlenecks and constraints in their value stream process on a regular basis?
{id: Q222} Does the team regularly work on ways to improve bottlenecks and constraints?
{id: Q223} Does the team track these improvement ideas in their backlog?

Description: All files needed to build the application are managed in version control. This includes build configuration files, such as makefiles and project files, and any custom build scripts. There is a defined build environment used by all central builds and available to engineers. Ideally, the build environment will be a virtual machine (VM) image or container image, but it may be a list of package versions required to successfully build. The build system generates deployable artifacts, e.g., container images, VM images, Operating System (OS) packages. If the application is to be delivered to a Cross Domain Solution (CDS), then this step may be manual, but it should be defined and repeatable. The version of the source code in version control used to generate released builds, i.e., versions of the application that are handed off to groups outside the product team, is tagged or labeled in the version control system. Ideally, it is possible to identify which version of the build environment was used to run the build.
Prerequisites: Capability: Version Control for Application Source Code
Questions: {id: Q22} Is there a defined and/or automated process for creating a build environment for the application?
{id: Q23} Is there a defined and/or automated build procedure for the application?
{id: Q24} Does the build procedure generate deployable artifacts, (e.g., container images, VM images, OS packages), without additional manual steps after the build is complete?

{id: Q25} Is it possible to build deployable artifacts for the application given only (a) a build environment, (b) a copy of the source code from the central shared code repository, and (c) the build procedure?

{id: Q26} Given a release (i.e., a set of deployable artifacts, built for use outside the product team) from a previous build, is it possible to reproduce the version of source code used to build the release?

Description: Several environments may be used to build, test, and deploy the application. The configuration and purpose of each environment must be documented. This helps ensure that conflicting requirements are not placed on any environment. For example, an environment used for customer acceptance testing requires high-stability, which would be incompatible with the environmental requirements for high-impact testing such as dynamic security testing.
Questions: {id: Q159} Have all the environments used to develop, test, and deliver the application been defined and documented?
{id: Q160} Are all changes made to each environment documented and tracked?
{id: Q161} Have the activities performed in each environment been defined and documented?
{id: Q162} Have the activities performed in the same environment been confirmed not to conflict with each other?
{id: Q163} Are the team members aware of how each environment is intended to be used?

Description: The product team includes operations engineers. The operations engineers should fully participate in team activities such as work estimation, planning, testing, and retrospectives. Operations engineers should also assist the team in planning for and performing operations activities such as installation and deployment planning, patching, and system monitoring.
Prerequisites: Capability: Testing/Quality Assurance (QA) Involved in Cross-Functional Team
Questions: {id: Q119} Does the team include dedicated operations engineers?
{id: Q120} Do the operations engineers participate as full members of the team in Agile team activities?
{id: Q305} Do they participate in team planning?
{id: Q306} Do the operations engineers participate in designing and developing testing?
{id: Q307} Do the operations engineers participate in threat modeling?
{id: Q308} Do the operations engineers participate in team retrospectives?
{id: Q121} Does the entire team contribute to operations (e.g., installation and deployment planning)?
{id: Q122} Does the team self-identify operational needs (e.g., load balancing, monitoring) in the system design?

Description:
The CI build deploys to a staging environment where the customer can evaluate the current state of the application. The staging environment is created fresh for each build, using Infrastructure as Code (IaC) techniques with version-controlled files defining the staging environment, including networking, security, resource allocation, logging, and all other operational aspects of the application. 

Not every build will be deployed to the staging environment. The product owner will coordinate with the team and the customer to determine a schedule or other strategy for updating the staging environment, and the pipeline will only deploy approved builds to the staging environment. 

This capability extends the scope of the application from just the functionality implemented in the codebase to the full environment, including operational aspects. The codebase, through cloud-specific configuration management systems such as CloudFoundation (CF), Azure Resource Manager (ARM) templates, and through cloud-independent systems such as Ansible, defines not only the base functionality being implemented, but also the operational aspects, including but not limited to: 

Network architecture 

Network security 

Bastion hosts 

Load balancers 

Application scaling 

Gateways 

Backend databases 

Redundancy, both local and geographical 

Data backup 

Logging and monitoring 

The cross-functional team includes Operations engineers who are responsible for these operational aspects of the application. 

This capability applies when the target deployment environment for the application can be software-defined, in particular, if the target environment is a cloud. Embedded applications and other types of applications may have similar software-defined targets. For example, an embedded application may be able to run on a simulator. This capability is about creating a deployment of the application that can be assessed by the customer.
Questions: {id: Q237} Does the CI pipeline create a sample deployment of the application including the environment?
{id: Q238} Does the customer or customer representative have access to the sample deployment of the application?

Description:
Most applications depend on third-party packages that are pulled from repositories on the public internet. This includes items such as language specific packages, OS Specific packages, and public library source code from GitHub. Few, if any, projects create source code for all the functionalities being delivered, instead choosing to use existing, tried-and-true solutions. This choice significantly accelerates development – since engineers do not need to implement common functionality such as protocol stacks – and improves quality – since engineers can use mature open-source code solutions that have been used, inspected, and tested over many years.

However, dependence on external packages and external package repositories can cause significant problems:

The exact versions of packages available in external repositories can change. If the application explicitly depends on a particular version, then if the external repository changes, the application becomes unbuildable until the issue is resolved.

Package version dependencies in external repositories can change over time. If the application does not specify dependence on particular versions for some or all packages that are used, then a relatively minor dependency change in external package dependencies can lead to an unreconcilable set of package versions in the application.

If an application uses the latest version of a package, then changes in a newer version of the package can break the build or the application. If the latest version is downloaded without being reviewed and tested prior to the build, then the build or application can break or change in unexpected ways even if the codebase does not change, making it difficult to detect and track issues.

If the application can only use packages that have been scanned for security vulnerabilities, but it also pulls packages from external repositories, there is typically no simple way to track what packages have been pulled and to be sure that every package version has been scanned and approved. A small change to the codebase might inadvertently pull in a new package or package version.

Networking or other external issues outside the control of the product team or organization can stop the build from working. If the external gateway is attacked by a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, this can stop builds from fetching packages and therefore break the builds. If an external organization changes its policies around repository access (for example Docker changed the policy around image pulls in 2020) then this can break the build.

The solution to these problems is to maintain an internal cache of all external packages. The cache is managed so that all artifacts in the cache are scanned and approved, and so that newer versions of packages are added in a defined and controlled manner. There are typically separate dated caches, such that the application will depend on one dated cache at any point in time, and will move up to a later dated cache containing some updated and/or new packages in a controlled manner. Private engineer builds can still fetch packages directly from the internet, but central builds run disconnected from the internet. If an engineer starts to use a new package or package version, then they are responsible for requesting that the new package be added to the appropriate cache along with any required approvals.

Internally generated artifacts such as container images, VM images, and OS packages, are managed in managed artifact repositories. Where there are dependencies between codebases (i.e., if codebase A builds a library used by codebase B) then the built artifacts are stored in the repository along with sufficient information to record the version of source code used to build the artifacts, including all required dependencies. In this way, the complete set of codebase and package versions required to build or run a particular version of an application is known.
Questions: {id: Q151} Does the pipeline run the build in an environment that is isolated from resources external to the organization?
{id: Q152} For each package in the internal cache, is the source of that package documented?

{id: Q153} Are the products of a pipeline build saved and managed so that they can be retrieved and deployed after the pipeline build is completed (i.e., are they saved in an artifact management system)?  Note: the “artifact management system” can be as simple as a filesystem.
{id: Q154} Is there a retention policy for build products?

Description: One purpose of Agile and Development, Security, and Operations (DevSecOps) practices is to maximize opportunities for feedback. To accomplish this goal, the team delivers and deploys small batches of value to the customer at regular intervals to elicit feedback.
Questions: {id: Q70} Does the product team demonstrate value to the customer frequently?
{id: Q71} Does the product team deliver and deploy small batches of changes to the customer?
